entities.name: Konrad VI the Dean
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Konrad VI the Dean (died 1427-09-12) emerged as a pivotal figure in late medieval Silesia, simultaneously holding the titles of Duke of Oleśnica, Koźle, half of Bytom, and half of Ścinawa from 1416, while also serving as the esteemed Dean of Wrocław Cathedral. Born into the Oleśnica branch of the Piast dynasty, a lineage critical to Central European history, his unique dual role as both a secular sovereign and a high-ranking ecclesiastical dignitary positioned him at the intricate nexus of temporal and spiritual power in a region often contested between the Kingdom of Bohemia and the Kingdom of Poland. His life exemplifies the complex strategies of medieval nobility to secure influence and patrimony through both dynastic succession and the institutional might of the Church, particularly within the fragmented landscape of the Silesian duchies.

Upon the death of his father, Konrad III the Old, in 1412, Konrad VI initially co-ruled with his brothers, inheriting his specific ducal territories in 1416 alongside Konrad V Kantner, Jan I, and Konrad VII the White. As Dean of Wrocław Cathedral, a prominent ecclesiastical seat, Konrad VI wielded significant administrative and spiritual authority, which he strategically leveraged to bolster his family's position and influence within his secular domains. His governance involved navigating the delicate balance of maintaining ducal autonomy while managing feudal obligations and regional alliances, a common challenge for Silesian Piasts in the shadow of the powerful Bohemian crown, to which many Silesian duchies were feoffed.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Konrad VI the Dean's dual role as a duke and a high-ranking cleric highlights the complex power structures of late medieval Silesia, influencing the local political and ecclesiastical landscape through his administrative actions and territorial holdings. His life exemplifies the strategies of the Piast dynasty in navigating fragmented rule and external pressures, though his direct impact was limited to his specific ducal territories and the Wrocław diocese.
